name: Ahab
charge: Marrying Jezebel; serving Baal; sparing Ben-hadad whom the Lord appointed to destruction
summary: Ahab did more to provoke the Lord than all the kings before him: he married a Zidonian, built Baal a house in Samaria, and made a grove. He spared the king of Syria for a trade deal after the Lord gave him the victory, and sold himself to work wickedness in Naboth's vineyard.
offense: Ahab treated walking in Jeroboam's sins as a light thing and added service to Baal. He married Jezebel, built a house and altar for Baal in Samaria, and made a grove, provoking the Lord above the kings before him (1 Kings 16:30-33). The inherited corruption became the foundation for further departure rather than a warning to turn back. During the famine he called Elijah the troubler of Israel. Elijah returned the charge to Ahab and his father's house for forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:17-18). The king blamed the bearer of the warning for the distress produced by his own course. Killing the messenger or silencing him could not restore the rain. The Lord afterward delivered the Syrians into his hand, declaring that Israel would know him as the Lord. Ahab received Ben-hadad as a brother and released him under a covenant promising restored cities and trading streets (1 Kings 20:28-34). The prophet answered that Ahab had let go a man appointed to destruction; his life would answer for that life (1 Kings 20:42). A useful agreement did not authorize setting aside the judgment. When Naboth refused his vineyard, Ahab withdrew in displeasure. Jezebel arranged false witnesses and Naboth's death, and Ahab went down to take possession (1 Kings 21:1-16). Elijah met him there and joined the acts in one charge: killing and taking possession. Ahab's benefit from the murder was not separated from its guilt because another person organized it.
judgment: Elijah pronounced the cutting off of Ahab's house and the consuming of its dead by dogs and birds. Ahab rent his clothes, fasted, wore sackcloth, and went softly. The Lord regarded his humbling and deferred the evil upon his house to his son's days (1 Kings 21:20-29). Mercy was shown within the judgment, without declaring his earlier deeds acceptable. At Ramoth-gilead, Micaiah warned that Israel would be scattered as sheep without a shepherd. Ahab imprisoned him and went to battle in disguise (1 Kings 22:17, 26-30). He sought safety through changing his appearance while refusing to change the course against which the word had spoken. An archer drawing at a venture struck him between the joints of his armour. He died that evening, and dogs licked his blood when the chariot was washed at Samaria (1 Kings 22:34-38). Neither a royal army nor a disguise could keep the sentence from finding him. His house continued for a time, but the king himself did not return in the peace he had demanded from his prophets.

verses.text: And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord above all that were before him.

And it came to pass, as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, that he took to wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, and went and served Baal, and worshipped him.
And he reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria.
And Ahab made a grove; and Ahab did more to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger than all the kings of Israel that were before him.
And it came to pass, when Ahab saw Elijah, that Ahab said unto him, Art thou he that troubleth Israel?
And he answered, I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father’s house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the Lord, and thou hast followed Baalim.

And his servants said unto him, Behold now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings: let us, I pray thee, put sackcloth on our loins, and ropes upon our heads, and go out to the king of Israel: peradventure he will save thy life.

So they girded sackcloth on their loins, and put ropes on their heads, and came to the king of Israel, and said, Thy servant Ben–hadad saith, I pray thee, let me live. And he said, Is he yet alive? he is my brother.

Now the men did diligently observe whether any thing would come from him, and did hastily catch it: and they said, Thy brother Ben–hadad. Then he said, Go ye, bring him. Then Ben–hadad came forth to him; and he caused him to come up into the chariot.

And Ben–hadad said unto him, The cities, which my father took from thy father, I will restore; and thou shalt make streets for thee in Damascus, as my father made in Samaria. Then said Ahab, I will send thee away with this covenant. So he made a covenant with him, and sent him away.

And he said unto him, Thus saith the Lord, Because thou hast let go out of thy hand a man whom I appointed to utter destruction, therefore thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people.
But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the Lord, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.
And he did very abominably in following idols, according to all things as did the Amorites, whom the Lord cast out before the children of Israel.
And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly.
And the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,
Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me? because he humbleth himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days: but in his son’s days will I bring the evil upon his house.

And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: wherefore he said unto the driver of his chariot, Turn thine hand, and carry me out of the host; for I am wounded.
And the battle increased that day: and the king was stayed up in his chariot against the Syrians, and died at even: and the blood ran out of the wound into the midst of the chariot.
And there went a proclamation throughout the host about the going down of the sun, saying, Every man to his city, and every man to his own country.
So the king died, and was brought to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria.
And one washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria; and the dogs licked up his blood; and they washed his armour; according unto the word of the Lord which he spake.
And when the Lord thy God shall deliver them before thee; thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them:
Neither shalt thou make marriages with them; thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son.
For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods: so will the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, and destroy thee suddenly.

entries.commentary: The word of the Most High comes to Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha, because though he was exalted out of the dust and made prince over Israel, he walked in the way of Jeroboam and made Israel sin. Therefore the Most High will make his house like the house of Jeroboam, and those who die in the city the dogs will eat and those in the field the fowls will eat. The same judgment falls because the same sin is repeated, just as descendants keep the pattern of their fathers though they saw the ruin it brought.

Elah son of Baasha reigns two years, and his servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspires against him while he is drunk in a steward's house and kills him. Zimri, on taking the throne, slays all the house of Baasha, leaving not one male, according to the word spoken by Jehu against Baasha. All of it comes for the sins of Baasha and Elah, who provoked the Most High to anger with their vanities. -

Zimri reigns only seven days in Tirzah. When the people encamped against Gibbethon hear he has slain the king, they make Omri, captain of the host, king over Israel. Omri and Israel go up and besiege Tirzah, and when Zimri sees the city taken, he burns the king's house over himself and dies. His death comes for his sins in walking in the way of Jeroboam, and his treason is recorded, treason being punishable by death in that time.

Israel is divided: half follow Tibni son of Ginath and half follow Omri, but Omri's followers prevail, Tibni dies, and Omri reigns. Omri buys the hill Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, builds the city, and names it after Shemer. Omri does worse than all before him, walking in the way of Jeroboam, then sleeps with his fathers, and Ahab his son reigns in his place.

Ahab son of Omri reigns twenty-two years in Samaria and does evil above all that were before him. As if walking in Jeroboam's sins were a light thing, he takes Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians to wife and serves and worships Baal, rearing an altar and a grove, provoking the Most High more than all the kings before him. This mirrors Solomon, who followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and the marrying outside the people that the law forbids because it turns the heart to other gods. In his days Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho, laying its foundation in his firstborn Abiram and setting up its gates in his youngest Segub, according to the word spoken by Joshua. -

After many days the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year: Go show thyself unto Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth. There was a sore famine in Samaria. Ahab called Obadiah, governor of his house, who feared the Lord greatly; when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah took an hundred prophets and hid them by fifty in a cave and fed them with bread and water, putting his own life in danger to save them. The famine was so sore it was hitting the animals, so Ahab and Obadiah divided the land between them, each going his own way to seek fountains and brooks to find grass to save the horses and mules alive. This was the fruit of the drought Elijah had pronounced.

As Obadiah went his way, Elijah met him; Obadiah fell on his face and said, Art thou my lord Elijah? Elijah told him to go tell Ahab that Elijah is here. Obadiah was afraid, for Ahab had searched every nation and kingdom to find and slay Elijah; that is how badly Jezebel wanted him dead, so she got Ahab to do her bidding. This is why Elijah had been on the run, first by Jordan, then years with the widow. Obadiah feared that the spirit of the Lord would carry Elijah away and Ahab would slay him for a false report, so he pleaded his own record: he feared the Lord from his youth and had hidden a hundred of the Lord's prophets by fifty in a cave. Elijah swore by the Lord of hosts that he would surely show himself to Ahab that day, and so Obadiah went to Ahab, and Ahab came to meet Elijah.

When Ahab saw Elijah he said, Art thou he that troubleth Israel? That is the mind of a wicked person: he blamed the trouble on the ordained prophet of God rather than on his own wickedness. When the spirit is gone, wisdom cannot enter a malicious soul, so Ahab had thoughts without understanding. Elijah answered, I have not troubled Israel, but thou and thy father's house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the Lord and thou hast followed Baalim. It was Ahab following the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, worshipping the golden calves, that brought the trouble. Elijah commanded that all Israel be gathered to Mount Carmel with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves that eat at Jezebel's table. Jezebel was the one feeding these eight hundred and fifty false prophets and encouraging them, and Ahab never checked her.

Ahab gathered the prophets and all Israel to Mount Carmel, and Elijah said unto the people, How long halt ye between two opinions? If the Lord be God, follow him, but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word. That is a call for all of us to examine ourselves: cast away every burden and sin and follow the Most High and his son fully, keeping the commandments, and do not keep one foot in and one foot out. Being lukewarm, playing the middle ground, ends with Christ spewing a man out of his mouth, and the next step after that is death. Elijah proposed the test: let each side dress a bullock, lay it on wood, and put no fire under, and the God that answereth by fire, let him be God. All the people said, It is well spoken.

The prophets of Baal dressed their bullock first and called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, O Baal, hear us, but there was no voice nor any that answered, and they leaped upon the altar. Picture the scene: eight hundred and fifty men doing this, running wild, while Elijah sat back watching the madness. At noon Elijah mocked them, saying, Cry aloud, for he is a god; either he is talking, or pursuing, or on a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth and must be awaked. They cried aloud and cut themselves with knives and lancets till the blood gushed out, for cutting themselves was part of their false worship whenever they called on Baal. From midday past the time of the evening sacrifice there was neither voice nor any to answer nor any that regarded. No one answered because the Most High will not give his glory to another, and the gods of the nations are idols that are not real; they are made up by people who have no God, so when they call on them the idols cannot answer.

Elijah repaired the altar of the Lord with twelve stones according to the twelve tribes of the sons of Jacob, made a trench about it, laid the wood and the bullock in order, and had them drench the sacrifice with four barrels of water three times until the water filled the trench. At the time of the evening sacrifice Elijah prayed, Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel and that I am thy servant. As the law appointed a sacrifice in the morning and in the evening, this was the evening sacrifice as the sun went down. Elijah prayed, Hear me, O Lord, that this people may know that thou art the Lord God and that thou hast turned their heart back again. Then the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water in the trench. When all the people saw it they fell on their faces and cried, The Lord, he is the God; the Lord, he is the God. Elijah commanded, Take the prophets of Baal, let not one of them escape, and they were brought down to the brook Kishon and slain there. In the last days it will be the same: when the Most High rains down fire again by the hands of Christ, no false prophet of Baal will escape, for they that feed the sheep of God lies will not be able to flee.

Elijah told Ahab to get up and eat and drink, for there was a sound of abundance of rain. Ahab went up to eat while Elijah went to the top of Carmel, cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees to pray. Elijah sent his servant seven times to look toward the sea; at the seventh time he reported a little cloud out of the sea like a man's hand. Elijah sent word to Ahab to prepare his chariot and get down before the rain stopped him, for the hand of the Lord was coming. The heaven grew black with clouds and wind and there was a great rain; Ahab rode to Jezreel, a city in the north in Samaria, and the hand of the Lord was on Elijah so that he girded up his loins and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.

Ben-hadad the king of Syria gathered all his hosts, with thirty-two kings, horses, and chariots, and besieged Samaria. He sent to Ahab demanding his silver, gold, wives, and children, even the goodliest, and Ahab answered, My lord, O king, I am thine, and all that I have. Ben-hadad sent again, saying that his servants would come and search Ahab's house and take away whatsoever was pleasant in his eyes. This siege was Ahab's judgment from the Lord for trying to kill Elijah, for serving Baal, and for letting Jezebel run him and kill the prophets.

Ahab called the elders of the land, who told him not to hearken nor consent to Ben-hadad's demand, so Ahab sent word that he would grant the first demand but not the second. Ben-hadad swore by his gods to reduce Samaria to dust for handfuls among his people. Ahab answered, Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off. When Ben-hadad heard this while drinking with the kings in the pavilions, he commanded his servants to set themselves in array against the city; Ahab's boast had provoked him to prepare for battle.

A prophet came unto Ahab saying, Thus saith the Lord, Hast thou seen all this great multitude? I will deliver it into thine hand this day, and thou shalt know that I am the Lord. Asked by whom, the prophet answered, By the young men of the princes of the provinces, and that Ahab himself should order the battle. Two hundred and thirty-two young men of the princes of the provinces went out first, followed by the children of Israel, being seven thousand; they went out at noon while Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk with the thirty-two kings, taking Israel lightly. The young men slew every one his man and the Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them; Ben-hadad escaped on a horse, and the king of Israel smote the horses and chariots and slew the Syrians with a great slaughter. The Most High gave the victory though Israel's numbers were small.

The prophet warned Ahab to strengthen himself and mark, for at the return of the year the king of Syria would come up against him again. The servants of Ben-hadad counseled that Israel's gods were gods of the hills, so they should fight in the plain, replace the kings with captains, and number a fresh army horse for horse and chariot for chariot; Ben-hadad hearkened and did so. At the return of the year Ben-hadad came up to fight, and the children of Israel pitched before them like two little flocks of kids while the Syrians filled the country; Israel's army was small compared to the great Syrian host. A man of God told Ahab, Because the Syrians have said the Lord is God of the hills but not of the valleys, I will deliver all this great multitude into thine hand, and ye shall know that I am the Lord. Here the Most High was giving Ahab a chance to repent, redeeming him by showing his power with fewer numbers; yet Ahab still did not repent, did not check Jezebel, and did not destroy the idols of Baal, for his sin had blinded him. Israel and Syria pitched one against the other seven days, and on the seventh day the battle was joined, and the children of Israel slew of the Syrians a hundred thousand footmen in one day. The rest fled to Aphek, where a wall fell upon twenty-seven thousand of the men left. Seven thousand against a hundred thousand, and the numbers did not matter because the Lord was with Israel; but Ahab still did not repent.

Ben-hadad fled into an inner chamber, and his servants, having heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful, put sackcloth on their loins and ropes on their heads and went to plead for his life. Ahab, hearing that Ben-hadad lived, called him his brother and had him brought up into his chariot. Look at Ahab's wickedness: this was a Syrian who was just trying to kill him last year, and he brought him up into the king's chariot. Ben-hadad offered to restore the cities his father had taken and give Ahab streets in Damascus, and Ahab said, I will send thee away with this covenant, and he made a covenant with the heathen and sent him away.

A son of the prophets told his neighbor to smite him in the word of the Lord; the man refused, and the prophet said a lion would slay him for not obeying the voice of the Lord, and a lion found him and slew him. Another man smote and wounded him, and the prophet disguised himself with ashes on his face and waited for the king, hiding the certain look that prophets carry, the same way we carry a certain look today. The prophet cried to the king a parable of a soldier charged to keep a prisoner on pain of his own life, who let the man escape; the king of Israel judged, So shall thy judgment be, thou thyself hast decided it. Then the prophet took the ashes away and Ahab discerned he was one of the prophets. The prophet declared, Thus saith the Lord, because thou hast let go a man whom I appointed to utter destruction, thy life shall go for his life and thy people for his people. Ben-hadad was supposed to die at war with Ahab, tied to the word that Hazael would move into the kingship of Syria, but Ahab made a covenant with him instead of killing him. The king of Israel went to his house heavy and displeased and came to Samaria, crying again over a just judgment because he would not obey the voice of the Lord. The lesson for us is the same: as it is written, so shall we do, that we may be justified and our life not be taken from us for rebellion against the Lord. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

Naboth had a vineyard next to Ahab's palace in Jezreel, and Ahab asked to trade or buy it, offering a better vineyard or its worth in money. Naboth refused because the land was the inheritance of his fathers. He could not simply hand off an inheritance that was given to him. -

Ahab went home heavy and displeased, laid down on his bed, turned away his face, and would eat no bread. He threw a fit and sulked because he could not get his way, angry that a subject would not surrender his inheritance.

Jezebel came to Ahab and asked why his spirit was so sad that he would not eat, and he told her Naboth's refusal. Jezebel mocked his weakness, telling him he was king and should let his heart be merry, and she promised to get the vineyard of Naboth for him.

Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his seal, sending them to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city. The seal was a signet, an official mark of the king's authority, so the letters carried royal weight as if Ahab himself had written them. She commanded them to proclaim a fast, set Naboth on high, and set two sons of Belial before him to bear false witness that he blasphemed God and the king, then stone him. This was evil counsel and a murderous plot. -

The elders and nobles obeyed Jezebel's letters, proclaimed a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people. Two children of Belial, children of the devil, sat before Naboth and falsely witnessed that he had blasphemed God and the king. They carried Naboth out and stoned him to death, then sent word to Jezebel that he was dead.

When Jezebel heard Naboth was dead, she told Ahab to arise and take possession of the vineyard he had been refused. Ahab rose up and went down to take the vineyard. This is extortion, seizing what another has by violence and force. Ahab shares the guilt. He sat by and let Jezebel commit the crime because he coveted the field, then turned his face from the evil and went to claim the reward. -

The word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite to go down and meet Ahab in the vineyard of Naboth. Elijah was to declare, Thus saith the Lord, hast thou killed and also taken possession, and in the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, dogs would lick Ahab's own blood.

Ahab called Elijah his enemy, and Elijah answered that he had found him because Ahab had sold himself to work evil in the sight of the Lord. The Most High would bring evil on Ahab, cut off every male of his house, and make his house like the house of Jeroboam and the house of Baasha because of the provocation by which he made Israel to sin. The phrase him that pisseth against the wall refers to the males, whom the Most High said he would cut off entirely. -

The Most High declared that the dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel. Any of Ahab's house dying in the city the dogs would eat, and any dying in the field the fowls of the air would eat, matching the curses spoken in the law. -

There was none like Ahab, who sold himself to work wickedness in the sight of the Lord, stirred up by Jezebel his wife. He did very abominably in following idols, as did the Amorites whom the Most High cast out before the children of Israel.

When Ahab heard these words he rent his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, and went softly, humbling himself before the Most High. Because Ahab humbled himself, the Most High told Elijah he would not bring the evil in Ahab's own days but would bring it upon his house in his son's days. The judgment was not cancelled but delayed and transferred to the next generation, showing that genuine humbling before the Most High moves his hand. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement)

After three years without war between Syria and Israel, Jehoshaphat king of Judah comes down to the king of Israel. Ahab reminds his servants that Ramoth in Gilead belongs to Israel, yet they sit still and do not take it out of the hand of the king of Syria. Ahab asks Jehoshaphat to go with him to battle, and Jehoshaphat answers that he is as Ahab is, his people and horses as Ahab's, but first asks that they inquire at the word of the Lord. Ahab gathers about four hundred prophets, who all say with one mouth, go up, for the Lord shall deliver it into the hand of the king. This is the setting for a division that ran between the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom. After the split, the northern kingdom fell into idolatry and forsook the Levites, so a prophet of the Most High would want nothing to do with their manner of worship. -

Jehoshaphat is not moved by four hundred prophets speaking the same thing, and asks whether there is not yet a prophet of the Lord that they may inquire of him. He wants to hear from a true prophet of the Most High, not from prophets who serve the king. Ahab answers that there is one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, but he hates him because Micaiah does not prophesy good concerning him, but evil. Jehoshaphat rebukes him, saying, let not the king say so.

The king of Israel calls an officer to hasten Micaiah, while Ahab and Jehoshaphat sit each on his throne in their robes at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets prophesy before them. Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah makes horns of iron and says, thus saith the Lord, with these shalt thou push the Syrians until thou have consumed them. Here again a man claims to speak for the Most High while the whole company presses Ahab to go up and prosper.

The messenger tells Micaiah that all the prophets declare good to the king with one mouth, and urges him to speak likewise. Micaiah answers that whatever the Lord saith unto him, that will he speak, and at first he echoes the others, prompting the king to adjure him to tell nothing but the truth. Micaiah then reveals what he saw, all Israel scattered on the hills as sheep having no shepherd, and the Lord saying these have no master. He saw the Lord on his throne with all the host of heaven, and a spirit that offered to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab's prophets to persuade him to fall at Ramoth-gilead. The Most High put a lying spirit in the mouth of these prophets and spoke evil concerning Ahab. The deceiver as well as the deceived are under the hand of the Most High, who uses the lie to bring the judgment he has already declared. -

Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah smites Micaiah on the cheek and asks which way the spirit of the Lord went from him to speak to Micaiah, defending his own false prophecy. The king of Israel orders Micaiah taken back and put in prison, fed with bread and water of affliction until Ahab returns in peace. Micaiah answers that if Ahab returns at all in peace, the Lord has not spoken by him, and calls all the people to hearken. His word stands as the test of who truly spoke for the Most High.

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat go up to Ramoth-gilead. Ahab disguises himself and tells Jehoshaphat to wear his robes, hoping to escape the word spoken against him, while the king of Syria commands his captains to fight only against the king of Israel. The captains pursue Jehoshaphat until they perceive he is not the king of Israel and turn back. A certain man draws a bow at a venture and smites Ahab between the joints of the harness, and the king is held up in his chariot until he dies at even, the blood running into the chariot. When they wash the chariot in the pool of Samaria, the dogs lick up his blood according to the word of the Lord. The judgment pronounced earlier against Ahab and his house begins to be fulfilled exactly as spoken.

The rest of the acts of Ahab, the ivory house he made and the cities he built, are written in the book of the Chronicles of the kings of Israel. Ahab sleeps with his fathers, and Ahaziah his son reigns in his stead.

Jehoshaphat the son of Asa begins to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab, at thirty-five years old, and reigns twenty-five years in Jerusalem. He walks in the ways of Asa his father, doing right in the eyes of the Lord, though the high places are not taken away and the people still burn incense there. Jehoshaphat makes peace with the king of Israel and puts the remnant of the sodomites out of the land. There is then no king in Edom but a deputy, because Edom had been subdued and had not yet revolted. -

Ahaziah the son of Ahab begins to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat and reigns two years. He does evil in the sight of the Lord and walks in the way of his father and his mother and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin. He serves Baal and worships him and provokes the Lord God of Israel to anger, according to all that his father had done. The sin of the house of Ahab continues into the next generation. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The seven nations cast out before Israel, the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, greater and mightier than Israel, are Hamitic nations. Thou shalt smite them and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them. Since the days of old the Most High has never been about the love-of-the-world gospel; throw that doctrine in the trash. This is why they do not want you reading the old covenant: verses like this correct the miseducation received through Christianity, and the mind begins to correct itself as you read.

Neither shalt thou make marriages with them: the Most High forbids marrying outside the nation. The seed of the fathers today is found among the so-called blacks, Hispanics, and Native Indians, who make up the twelve tribes of Israel; a spouse may come from any of the twelve tribes, but from within the tribes only. Going outside your nation for a husband or wife is despising your brethren in your heart. Whom you marry is the greatest commitment you make in this life; if you truly loved your people, you would choose one of your own people to become aged together with. They will turn away thy son from following me: the nations are strangers to the Most High and cannot come into this covenant, so they draw the Israelite spouse off to religions that accept everything. Christianity accepts that union, and that is how they turn you away from your God.
Thus shall ye deal with them: destroy their altars, break down their images, cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire. Nothing of their worship was to be spared or adopted.

For thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God: this is one of the most uplifting scriptures in the book, and it should be etched into your children's minds from the moment they begin to read, until it is implanted into their spirit. The mind controls the body: what goes into the mind comes out through the body, so a people that knows it is holy and special above all people walks and carries itself differently. Being chosen above all people keeps you out of the affairs of this world, their fashions, their hairstyles, their trends and challenges, and keeping up with the Joneses; you cannot flip-flop with every new wave and still carry the speciality the Most High put on you.

The Lord did not choose Israel for their number, for ye were the fewest of all people: only threescore and ten souls came out of the loins of Jacob when Israel first went down, as Genesis records, some places reading seventy and some counting seventy-five. But because the Lord loved you: the Most High needs no other reason, he simply loved us, and we should never apologize for that. He kept the oath sworn unto the fathers and redeemed Israel out of the house of bondmen, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt; Israel came out from under Rameses.

Know therefore that the Lord thy God, he is God, the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations, and repayeth them that hate him to their face. This is the same teaching as the new testament: loving the Most High is keeping his commandments, and refusing his commandments shows him with your actions that you hate him, and then judgment comes. From the jump it has always been the same: love God, keep the commandments; nothing changed between the covenants.

If ye hearken to these judgments and keep and do them, the Lord keeps the covenant and the mercy: he will love thee, bless thee, and multiply thee, blessing the fruit of thy womb, thy land, thy corn, wine, oil, kine, and sheep, blessed above all people, which goes right back to verse 6. The Lord will take away from thee all sickness and put none of the evil diseases of Egypt upon thee, but will lay them upon all them that hate thee. That still reigns true today: keep the commandments and the Most High will keep you from the diseases of modern-day Egypt, and if you do catch something, he will revive you and bring you back to your health.

Thou shalt consume all the people which the Lord thy God shall deliver thee; thine eye shall have no pity upon them, neither shalt thou serve their gods, for that will be a snare unto thee. Those days are coming back when Christ returns.

If thou shalt say in thine heart, these nations are more than I: fear them not, but remember what the Lord did unto Pharaoh and unto all Egypt, the signs, the wonders, the mighty hand and the stretched out arm; so shall he do unto all the people of whom thou art afraid. The Lord will send the hornet among them until even those that hide themselves are destroyed, and he will put out those nations before thee by little and little, lest the beasts of the field increase upon thee. He shall deliver their kings into thine hand, and thou shalt destroy their name from under heaven. There is no way to read [Deuteronomy 7](/bible/deuteronomy/7) and still say God loves everybody; that idea is being drunk on Christianity, not reading the book.

The graven images of their gods shall ye burn with fire: desire not the silver or gold that is on them, lest thou be snared therein, for it is an abomination to the Lord thy God. Neither shalt thou bring an abomination into thine house, lest thou be a cursed thing like it. Bring it up to today: the Jesus pieces, the crosses, the ankhs, and the rosary beads wrapped around the neck and rubbed in prayer make the wearer an abomination and a cursed thing just like the idol. The main abomination we bring into our house is the Christmas tree of Jeremiah 10: the tree cut down, fastened with nails and hammers, and decked with silver and with gold, whether cut from the forest or bought as a fake tree from the store.

text.text: And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord above all that were before him.

And it came to pass, as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, that he took to wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, and went and served Baal, and worshipped him.
And he reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria.
And Ahab made a grove; and Ahab did more to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger than all the kings of Israel that were before him.
And it came to pass, when Ahab saw Elijah, that Ahab said unto him, Art thou he that troubleth Israel?
And he answered, I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father’s house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the Lord, and thou hast followed Baalim.

And his servants said unto him, Behold now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings: let us, I pray thee, put sackcloth on our loins, and ropes upon our heads, and go out to the king of Israel: peradventure he will save thy life.

So they girded sackcloth on their loins, and put ropes on their heads, and came to the king of Israel, and said, Thy servant Ben–hadad saith, I pray thee, let me live. And he said, Is he yet alive? he is my brother.

Now the men did diligently observe whether any thing would come from him, and did hastily catch it: and they said, Thy brother Ben–hadad. Then he said, Go ye, bring him. Then Ben–hadad came forth to him; and he caused him to come up into the chariot.

And Ben–hadad said unto him, The cities, which my father took from thy father, I will restore; and thou shalt make streets for thee in Damascus, as my father made in Samaria. Then said Ahab, I will send thee away with this covenant. So he made a covenant with him, and sent him away.

And he said unto him, Thus saith the Lord, Because thou hast let go out of thy hand a man whom I appointed to utter destruction, therefore thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people.
But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the Lord, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.
And he did very abominably in following idols, according to all things as did the Amorites, whom the Lord cast out before the children of Israel.
And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly.
And the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,
Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me? because he humbleth himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days: but in his son’s days will I bring the evil upon his house.

And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: wherefore he said unto the driver of his chariot, Turn thine hand, and carry me out of the host; for I am wounded.
And the battle increased that day: and the king was stayed up in his chariot against the Syrians, and died at even: and the blood ran out of the wound into the midst of the chariot.
And there went a proclamation throughout the host about the going down of the sun, saying, Every man to his city, and every man to his own country.
So the king died, and was brought to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria.
And one washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria; and the dogs licked up his blood; and they washed his armour; according unto the word of the Lord which he spake.
And when the Lord thy God shall deliver them before thee; thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them:
Neither shalt thou make marriages with them; thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son.
For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods: so will the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, and destroy thee suddenly.
